title: Odile and the Harvest
premise: Paloma Sterling, a nonbinary teacher who has spent seven years rationalizing the strange noises in their grandmother's farmhouse, returns to the family home when the local school's students begin vanishing one by one. The old photographs have changed: every image now contains an extra wooden chair, and the chair is moving closer to the camera. Paloma discovers the family's prosperity was bought generations ago through a bargain with the Count, a presence that collects a soul at every harvest, and that their grandmother has been hiding the debt by feeding it strangers. To break the cycle, Paloma must offer the Count something it cannot count—memory freely surrendered—and the novel ends with Paloma walking into the final photograph themselves, erasing their own name from every mind that loved them, while the family survives and the chairs disappear from all the pictures but one.
about_author: Silas Vasquez is the pen name of a former rural schoolteacher who taught for nine years in farm towns where the census never quite matched the number of desks. Their fiction draws on the quiet dread of communities that have learned not to ask questions.

chapters.title: Attendance
chapters.summary: Paloma, POV: taking roll on their first day back in Hollow Creek, they count twenty-two students but the register lists twenty-three, and no one will say who's missing. The emotional beat is the itch of a wrongness Paloma has trained themselves to ignore. Establishes the school's missing-class problem and Paloma's coping habit of explanation over intuition.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV: sorting grandma Odile's attic, they find the 1978 family portrait now shows a plain wooden chair that was never there. Every photo in the house has one. Odile's reaction—fear, then brisk denial—reveals she has seen this before. The beat is the collapse of Paloma's seven-year policy of rational explanations.

chapters.title: What the Well Kept
chapters.summary: Odile's POV: she remembers her own mother counting chairs at harvest and the bargain made in 1931, when the family's starving farm turned golden overnight. She has spent decades keeping the Count fed with drifters and transients so it would never come for kin. Guilt and fierce protectiveness war in her; she resolves to keep Paloma ignorant a little longer.

chapters.title: Empty Desks
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV: a third student, Marisol, stops attending, and the office has no record she ever enrolled. Her classmates half-remember her, then don't. Paloma finds Marisol's notebook with a child's drawing of a wooden chair and a tall figure counting on its fingers. Dread sharpens into resolve: Paloma starts asking questions the town won't answer.

chapters.title: The Counting Song
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV: at the harvest festival, children skip a number when singing the old counting rhyme—no one sings 'nine.' An elder tells Paloma, kindly and finally, to stop asking. That night the farmhouse noises return: footsteps that pause, as if counting rooms. The beat is the town's complicity made visible, and Paloma's isolation deepening.

chapters.title: Odile's Ledger
chapters.summary: Paloma, POV: searching Odile's locked trunk, they find a ledger of names—strangers, boarders, one per year, dated every autumn for ninety years—and a receipt written in a script that hurts to read. The last entry is blank, waiting. Horror becomes concrete: the family has been feeding people to the Count. Paloma's trust in Odile shatters.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Table
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, Paloma and Odile: the confrontation Paloma has been avoiding. Odile confesses the bargain but insists the alternative is the family itself—her parents tried to refuse in 1961 and the harvest took her brother instead. She begs Paloma to leave before the count finishes. The beat is love weaponized as secrecy, and Paloma's refusal to run alone.

chapters.title: The Chair Moves Closer
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV: the chair in the photographs has advanced—now it sits at the family's own dinner table in pictures taken last week. Paloma photographs the photos night by night and charts its approach like an eclipse. The beat is the horror of measurable inevitability: the Count is not coming for a stranger this year. It is coming for a Sterling.

chapters.title: Deputy Ruiz
chapters.summary: Deputy Ruiz's POV: a reluctant ally who has quietly kept a file of every missing drifter for twenty years but could never make the case stick—evidence literally unremembering itself. He gives Paloma the names and warns that the town's prosperity depends on the harvest. The beat is the theme of power's corruption: the whole town is a shareholder.

chapters.title: Nine
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV: reconstructing the counting song, Paloma realizes 'nine' was the Count's original name, struck from memory when it was bound to the bargain. Speaking it aloud makes the farmhouse lights gutter and every chair in the house turn to face the door. Names have power; the Count is not a demon but something older that was once counted among men. The beat is terrible discovery.

chapters.title: The Harvest Begins
chapters.summary: Odile's POV: the night of the equinox, the ledger's blank entry fills itself with Odile's own name. The bargain has noticed her aging out of usefulness. Odile accepts this with grim relief—her debt, her payment—until she finds the script has altered itself: the Count will take the youngest instead. Maternal terror overrides a lifetime of fatalism.

chapters.title: Paloma's Nephew
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV: seven-year-old Theo, visiting for the harvest, begins sleepwalking toward the well and drawing the chair from memory he shouldn't have. Paloma barricades the house and learns from the photographs that the chair now has an occupant—a shape like a man made of tally marks. The beat is protectiveness pushed to the edge of desperation.

chapters.title: The Well Room
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV: beneath the well, a root cellar holds ninety years of belongings—suitcases, glasses, a child's shoe—arranged in neat rows, each with a chair. The missing aren't dead; they're stored, half-remembered, part of the Count's collection. Paloma understands the price of survival: the family didn't kill anyone, they just let everyone else be forgotten. Moral horror replaces fear.

chapters.title: What Marisol Remembered
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV, from inside the collection: she exists in a fog where her name returns only when someone above speaks it. She has learned the collection's rule—the Count can only keep what is not freely given back. She claws toward the memory of her own name. The beat is fragile hope discovered in the story's darkest place.

chapters.title: The Town's Reckoning
chapters.summary: Deputy Ruiz's POV: Ruiz goes public with his file at the town meeting and is met not with shock but with bargaining—farmers offering up their own lists of names to protect their own. The corruption of power is laid bare: everyone knew, everyone profited, and they would feed the Count forever. Ruiz is run out of the meeting. The beat is disillusionment and clarity.

chapters.title: Odile's Last Lesson
chapters.summary: Odile's POV: she tells Paloma the full terms—the Count counts what it is owed, but it cannot count what is surrendered freely. Her mother's mistake in 1961 was refusing; refusal makes you a debt. Odile intends to walk to the well at midnight and give herself, but Paloma sees the loophole she's missed: it's not the life that must be given, it's the memory of the one who pays. The beat is inheritance transformed into strategy.

chapters.title: Preparations
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV: Paloma writes letters to everyone they love, then burns them, and begins deliberately unlearning—giving Odile and Theo the stories of their own childhood to keep, so the memories will survive even if Paloma doesn't. Theo, sharp and unafraid, asks to keep one: the song Paloma made up about his dinosaur. Tender, devastating preparation. The beat is love expressed as deliberate loss.

chapters.title: The Count Comes Home
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs: on the final night of harvest, the Count manifests in the farmhouse as the tally-marked man, polite and patient, seating itself in the extra chair at dinner. It speaks in the voices of the collected. It offers Paloma the old deal—give it Theo, and everything returns to normal. The beat is the temptation of the bargain, offered gently, and Paloma's refusal.

chapters.title: The Surrender
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV: instead of refusing to pay, Paloma pays differently—walking to the well and freely surrendering every memory of themselves, aloud, name first. The Count, bound to count what it is owed, must accept the gift and finds it cannot hold what is given away. The collection ruptures; the well room empties. Climax: the price of survival is paid in full, but in the one currency the Count cannot keep.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: Odile's POV: morning. The photographs are ordinary again, the ledger blank, the counting song whole. Marisol and the ninety years of missing come back to the town, remembering everything—and the town must finally face what it did. Odile grieves a grandchild whose name she can no longer hold onto, keeping only Theo's dinosaur song and a feeling like love. The beat is grief without an object.

chapters.title: The New Teacher
chapters.summary: Odile's and Ruiz's POVs: weeks later, a new teacher arrives at Hollow Creek school, friendly and unfamiliar, and takes roll—twenty-three names, all present. They pause at one name on the register that no one recognizes, a name written in a hand that hurts to read, and feel something like recognition. The beat is bittersweet ambiguity: survival, and its cost, walking among them.

chapters.title: One Chair
chapters.summary: Theo's POV, years later: the family thrives; the farm is ordinary; the Count is a story children half-remember. But in one photograph—Odile's last, found after her death—there is a single extra chair, empty, facing the camera, and beside it a place setting no one ever uses but no one ever removes. Theo sets it a plate at every harvest. The beat is the theme resolved: memory is the price, and love is how we pay it.
